overview: This file brings together U.S. State Department material on Japanese organized labor and employer-employee relations, beginning with the controversy surrounding a government Labor Union Bill in 1930 and ending with an internal 1933 note on labor conditions related to the Singer Sewing Machine Company dispute. Its largest component is a detailed 1934 consular report on the Japan Seamen’s Union, including its membership, finances, unemployment program, relations with shipowners and other unions, political influence, and demands for trade-union legislation, an eight-hour day, improved wages, safer manning, and better working conditions. The accompanying departmental memorandum emphasizes both the union’s unusually Western approach to collective bargaining and the possible consequences of higher Japanese operating costs for American shipping. Although the stated file dates end in 1933, pages 4–17 consist of material from 1934, illustrating the sometimes irregular accumulation or later filing of related records.

subfiles.title: File note on the proposed Labor Union Bill
subfiles.about: A filing note identifies a report on the government’s proposed Labor Union Bill and directs the reader to a related record.
subfiles.summary: The note records that the Japanese government had prepared a Labor Union Bill for submission to the next Diet session. It characterizes the public controversy as increasingly heated, with labor supporting the proposal and capital opposing it, and identifies report no. 45 as attached.

subfiles.title: Monthly report excerpt on the Labor Union Bill
subfiles.about: An excerpt from a monthly report describes press controversy over the proposed Labor Union Bill.
subfiles.summary: The report notes that few matters occupying public attention during June merited inclusion in the monthly review, but the Labor Union Bill was an exception. The press carried extensive controversy over the government’s plan to submit the bill to the Diet, with labor favoring it and capital resisting it. The author promises a further report if the dispute advances beyond its current verbal stage.

subfiles.title: Departmental summary of McClintock’s report on the Japan Seamen’s Union
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (apparently Eugene H. Dooman)
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum highlights the significance of the Japan Seamen’s Union meeting and recommends attention to its program.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum emphasizes the union’s declaration that Japan’s foreign-trade expansion rested on low wages, long hours, and workers’ sacrifices. It describes the union as Japan’s most important labor organization, containing about one-fourth of all union members. The writer contrasts the paternalistic legacy of industrial employment with seamen’s more Western preference for organization and group bargaining, and points out that higher Japanese vessel-operating costs could benefit American shipping interests.

subfiles.title: The Thirteenth Annual Meeting of the Japan Seamen’s Union
subfiles.from: Vice Consul Robert Mills McClintock, Kobe
subfiles.to: Commercial Office, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: A comprehensive consular report examines the membership, functions, finances, politics, and platform of Japan’s largest labor union.
subfiles.summary: McClintock presents the Japan Seamen’s Union as the country’s largest and most highly integrated union, with 98,612 members and an unusually strong position in maritime employment. He attributes maritime unionism partly to seamen’s freedom from older feudal craft traditions and their exposure to labor conditions under foreign flags, then surveys the union’s arbitration work, unemployment relief and insurance, cooperation and disputes with shipowners, political influence, and strong finances. The report reproduces demands for an eight-hour day, wage increases, bonuses, minimum manning levels, improved food and accommodations, retirement allowances, revision of the Seamen’s Code, and a national trade-union law. Its concluding resolution sharply challenges government and employer claims by arguing that Japanese trade competitiveness depended upon low wages and long hours.

subfiles.title: Internal note on Japanese labor conditions and the Singer dispute
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (initialed EHD)
subfiles.about: A brief departmental note summarizes a Tokyo consular report relevant to labor trouble involving the Singer Sewing Machine Company.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum records the Consulate General at Tokyo’s submission of a report on selected features of Japanese labor conditions. It identifies the report as relevant to difficulties involving the Singer Sewing Machine Company and singles out the assertion that employer-employee relations in Japan remained fundamentally feudal.

interest: The file is especially useful for the contrast between official Japanese representations of harmonious labor conditions and the seamen’s unusually candid claim that export success depended on low wages and long hours. McClintock’s report supplies rare quantitative and institutional detail—membership figures, unemployment benefits, finances, political alignments, and a full labor platform—while also revealing how U.S. officials interpreted Japanese labor through the lenses of feudal paternalism, Western collective bargaining, and commercial competition. The inclusion of 1934 documents in a nominally 1930–1933 file is also evidence of State Department filing practices and the continuing linkage of related labor questions.
